title: Runtime Topology & Tail Latency Workshop - Ark Robotics
summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail causes for Ark's inference workloads. Covered KV-cache hotkeys, inter-node network hops, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, batching windows, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a benchmark with Ark's 1k QPS mixed traffic and a follow-up network trace. Next steps include Redwood sending benchmark config, security docs, and a proposed pilot plan.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sasha Kim, Diego Ramos, Priya Khatri (Redwood); Evan Moore, Lydia Chen, Raj Patel, Maya Ortiz (Ark Robotics)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: discuss tail latency causes, propose benchmark and pilot.
Topics: see above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sasha Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for making time. i'm Sasha, i'll run the agenda quick — we want to map out the p95/p99 behaviour you saw in your staging run and walk through topology ideas. Diego will cover the runtime traces.
[00:27] Evan Moore: hey Sasha, yeah appreciate it. we've been seeing these weird p99 spikes on our command inference endpoint, usually around 200-400 ms while p95 stays nice around 80 to 120 ms. gives us some real user-facing jitter.
[00:45] Diego Ramos: ok got it, thanks Evan. quick clarifying q: are you seeing these spikes in both streaming and non-streaming endpoints or just generation?
[01:00] Raj Patel: mostly on the non-streaming batch endpoints used by our control stack; but sometimes the streaming chat path also shows microspikes when we hit concurrent long sequences.
[01:15] Diego Ramos: alright, that's helpful. i'll share my screen with the flame traces we recorded last week from Redwood's profiler — note that those traces were from a dedicated node sim matching your shape but might have slightly different network topology.
[01:30] Maya Ortiz: when you say dedicated node sim — is that a Redwood Dedicated cluster in us-west or sim'd on a GCP overlay?
[01:40] Diego Ramos: it's Redwood Dedicated in us-west-2, GPUs are A100-ish, we used kernel-level timers + network timestamps.
[01:52] Lydia Chen: cool. i'll say upfront our environment is VPC with a peering to a private colo where our on-prem telemetry lives. so we have a few extra network hops compared to pure cloud.
[02:05] Sasha Kim: that's an important detail — extra hops commonly show up in the tail, especially with KV cache misses.
[02:15] Diego Ramos: yes, first slide: p95 vs p99 waterfall. you can see the p95 cluster around 85ms: tokenization ~3ms, runtime forward ~40ms, postproc ~12ms, network ~15ms. p99 adds an extra 150-300ms blob often attributed to two classes: KV-cache miss + cross-node rehydration, and network retransmit/dns/peering queuing.
[02:41] Raj Patel: can you expand on the KV side — we use a small prefix cache we built, but it's mostly LRU on the client. how does Redwood's KV prefix caching differ?
[02:55] Diego Ramos: Redwood keeps per-model KV shards with sticky routing; within a node we maintain hot-cache in GPU memory (KV cache ring) and a fallback to a nearline memcached-like store. The common p99 case we see is a hotkey—lots of requests target a tiny set of prefixes -> evictions + cross-node fetch. The fetch path creates extra RPCs and a blocking wait, that's the 100-250ms.
[03:22] Evan Moore: we actually have a very skewed prefix distribution — our nav prompts are almost identical for 40% of requests. that sounds like hotkey.
[03:33] Diego Ramos: yep. two quick mitigations: 1) increase local hot-KV capacity or reserve pinning for the top N prefixes, 2) use routing to send the hot prefixes to a smaller set of nodes (reduces cross-node fetch probability). both trade throughput balance vs tail.
[03:52] Lydia Chen: pinning sounds great but we'd worry about capacity overcommit. can Redwood do a reserved pin on Dedicated pools?
[04:02] Sasha Kim: yes, Redwood Dedicated supports KV pinning and you can configure reserved capacity on a per-model routing rule — we've used that for other customers with skewed distributions. i'll add the config doc after the call.
[04:15] Raj Patel: ok. second area — streaming vs non-streaming. we've assumed streaming would always reduce tail because tokens are flushed earlier, but we've seen the opposite in some cases.
[04:29] Diego Ramos: good point. streaming reduces perceived latency because the first tokens arrive earlier, but it can increase overall p99 for full-response metrics if the streaming path relies on micro-batching or if there's a streaming buffer that waits to coalesce tokens. Also edge cases: if network MTU or tcp window interactions cause partial packet delays, streaming amplifies jitter.
[04:54] Maya Ortiz: we've got MTU and some middleboxes in our colo. could that explain microspikes?
[04:59] Diego Ramos: definitely. middleboxes that reassemble or inspect traffic can create 20-200ms of extra latency for certain flows. We'll want to run packet traces.
[05:11] Evan Moore: Diego, you mentioned batching windows — how do you set the window for low tail vs high throughput?
[05:19] Diego Ramos: Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with two knobs: max-latency window (e.g., 3ms-30ms) and max-batch size. For low p99 you set a very small window and accept lower throughput; for cost efficiency you can increase window. There's also adaptive mode where the runtime auto-tunes windows based on observed latency SLOs.
[05:39] Lydia Chen: do you have numbers showing p99 vs throughput at 3ms vs 20ms window?
[05:45] Diego Ramos: quick off-the-cuff from our lab: at 1k QPS mixed seq lengths, 3ms window gave p95 70ms p99 140ms, throughput ~0.8x; 20ms window p95 95ms, p99 220ms, throughput ~1.4x. numbers vary by model and quantization.
[06:05] Raj Patel: quantization — we ran int8 offline and saw some generation slowdowns on longer context lengths. thought quantization should speed things up.
[06:15] Priya Khatri: quantization usually reduces compute per token, but it can change kernel selection and force fallback paths for certain ops if they aren't quantized. Also memory layout changes can impact KV serialization time. In practice int8 often helps throughput and p95 but may slightly hurt p99 if it causes more cache pressure or extra conversions.
[06:37] Evan Moore: interesting. so int8 could reduce median but still spike p99 because of extra memory moves.
[06:43] Diego Ramos: exactly. we advise running a mixed-run A/B because some models behave differently. Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations by workload; we'll include a recommended profile for your model.
[06:55] Maya Ortiz: on the network hop side — we have VPC in cloud and a private colo for sensors. requests route through a transit gateway, then into colo. sometimes we see a 50–70ms jump which lines up with the p99. could the transient peering queueing cause reorders?
[07:12] Diego Ramos: yes, egress queuing and peering rate-limiting can create burst-induced latency. Also if there's any NAT gateway scaling or autoscaling lag it can add jitter. We recommend collecting histograms per hop and correlating p99 across layers: client -> edge ingress -> runtime node -> storage.
[07:31] Lydia Chen: we can provide a traceroute and VPC flow logs. will that be enough?
[07:36] Sasha Kim: flow logs help, and if you can capture tcpdump or perf counters around spikes that's gold. Diego will send a minimal packet-capture guide.
[07:46] Raj Patel: what about cross-region fallbacks — if a Redwood node in preferred region is saturated and you fall back to another region, how much tail do we typically see?
[07:58] Diego Ramos: cross-region fallback is last resort. latency penalty depends on distance + any vpn/peering overhead; p99 delta often 100-300ms. Redwood supports regional preference with warm standby nodes to reduce cold fallback. For Ark with stringent SLOs i'd suggest a warm standby in your closest region to avoid cross-region hops.
[08:20] Evan Moore: okay, that's doable. question: can we simulate our exact skew and routing to get a reliable estimate?
[08:28] Diego Ramos: yes — we'll use your workload trace to seed the bench. we have a harness that replays qps and sequence length distribution, plus the same prefix skew. the benchmark will collect token-level latencies and kernel timings.
[08:40] Lydia Chen: what's the overhead of enabling detailed kernel traces? we prefer not to impact production.
[08:46] Diego Ramos: the profiler has low overhead sampling mode that's safe for production; full tracing is heavier so we run it in staging. for production we'd recommend sampling 1% of requests or trigger traces only when latency crosses threshold.
[08:59] Raj Patel: another item — serialization between GPU and host for KV cache looks like a hotspot in your trace. any notes?
[09:07] Diego Ramos: yes, if KV entries are stored in a layout that requires copy+reshape on every fetch, that adds 10-30ms per miss. Memory-aligned KV layouts and zero-copy paths reduce this. Redwood runtime has a new zero-copy path for certain models — we can test with your model but may need a small model conversion.
[09:27] Evan Moore: model conversion — how invasive? we don't want drift in logits.
[09:33] Priya Khatri: conversions are deterministic; we maintain bit-exact inference where possible, otherwise we document any tiny numeric diffs and run eval suites. For Ark's controller models we'll recommend a conversion and eval set.
[09:47] Maya Ortiz: security: if we do Dedicated or Private, we need SSO, KMS, and audit logs. how does Redwood handle KMS in Private clusters?
[09:56] Sasha Kim: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. audit logs are available via your SIEM. i'll put the SOC2 plus Private deployment security notes in the email.
[10:07] Evan Moore: thanks. back to latency — Diego, can you summarise recommended immediate mitigations we can try without infra changes?
[10:14] Diego Ramos: short list: 1) increase sampling to identify hot prefixes, 2) enable pinning for the top 1% prefixes, 3) lower batching window for critical low-latency route, 4) run an int8 A/B test with monitoring on memory copy times, 5) collect network pcap and flow logs for spikes.
[10:33] Lydia Chen: will pinning require adding capacity?
[10:36] Diego Ramos: depends on pin count; we can simulate your distribution first. often pinning a small subset of very hot prefixes uses <10% extra memory if done carefully.
[10:45] Sasha Kim: i'll own sending the pinning config and the Redwood runner script.
[10:50] Raj Patel: great. any notes on observability? how do we get token-level latencies?
[10:55] Priya Khatri: Redwood console has token-level timing, per-route breakdowns and kernel flamegraphs; we'll set up a read-only view for Ark. also expose traces via open telemetry collector.
[11:08] Evan Moore: sounds good.
[11:12] [~11:12] short cross talk; attendees confirming next steps
[11:20] Diego Ramos: quick technical aside on batching and tail: some customers actually use two service tiers: a streaming-low-latency path with small window and a batched-high-throughput path with larger window. requests are routed by SLA token. helps keep p99 low for critical calls while keeping cost efficient batching for background work.
[11:41] Lydia Chen: routing by SLA — do we need change at app level?
[11:44] Sasha Kim: only a header flag, Redwood supports per-route policies so you can expose two endpoints.
[11:50] Raj Patel: i recall you also have a fallback policy that auto-switches model variants if a quantized variant is causing errors. is that safe?
[11:59] Diego Ramos: yes, there's automatic fallback to a float32 model variant if quality regressions detected or if a node reports errors. it's controlled by rollout policies.
[12:07] Evan Moore: one more question on KV sharding — is sticky session required to keep cache locality?
[12:12] Diego Ramos: sticky routing helps; we also do consistent hashing so that cache movements are minimized during autoscaling. sticky sessions plus consistent hashing gives best locality for hot prefixes.
[12:24] Maya Ortiz: ok we'll need to review our autoscaler settings.
[12:27] Sasha Kim: final wrap — to recap: Redwood will run a seeded benchmark using Ark's traces, provide pinning config, and share security docs. Ark will share VPC diagram, flow logs, and run tcpdump when requested. we'll reconvene with results.
[12:43] Evan Moore: thanks everyone, appreciate the level of detail.
[12:46] Lydia Chen: thanks.
[12:48] meeting ended
